939.title: The hardest gift
939.hook: the traditions speak of forgiveness, and none of them pretends it's easy
939.carry: sending a guard away from his post
939.howItsDone: Forgiveness is taught across the traditions: in Jewish practice around the Days of Awe, in Christian prayer, in Islamic teaching on pardon, and in Buddhist practices of loving-kindness, each with its own understanding of who forgives and how.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sabbath: the end of our weeks on work. Your line was work well, then rest. Did you finish one thing well, and then actually stop? Today, a new question, and a harder one. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

Some names land like a small stone in the chest. A parent. An old friend. A business partner. An ex. Years go by, and the stone is still there, and somebody says, kindly, just let it go. The obvious question is: how, exactly? That question opens the next stretch of this path. For the coming weeks we'll hear what the traditions say about forgiveness: Jewish voices first, then others, one at a time. And before any of them speaks, one thing worth saying plainly. The texts we're about to visit don't pretend it's easy.
screen: `A STONE IN THE CHEST.` → `JUST LET IT GO. HOW?` → `NOBODY SAYS IT'S EASY.`

segments.voice: First, why call it a gift. Forgiving gives something away: the right to get even, the story where you're owed. Nobody can force it out of you. That's what makes it a gift, and that's what makes it hard. Second, two old voices. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in a single line: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love", and it calls this an old rule. The Qur'an, in a verse about answering a wrong, allows a response in kind, then says that whoever pardons and makes peace, their reward is with God. Neither voice pretends the hurt didn't happen. Both point past it. Third, what forgiveness is not. Some teachers today, from more than one tradition, draw a line between forgiving and excusing. Forgiving doesn't say it was fine. It doesn't mean pretending to forget. And for some, it doesn't mean walking back into the same room with the same person. The traditions draw these lines in different places, and we'll hear them out one by one: whether the one who did wrong has to ask first, who is able to forgive what, and whether forgiving means making up. Fourth, why it's hard. Anger is often doing a job. It guards a wound. It keeps a record, so the thing won't happen again. Asking it to stand down can feel like sending a guard away from his post. That's why, on this path, forgiveness is treated as a practice, not a switch. It might take one try. It might take a great many.
screen: `A GIFT NOBODY CAN FORCE.` · `HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.` · `FORGIVING ISN'T EXCUSING.` · `ANGER GUARDS A WOUND.` · then, large: `THE HARDEST GIFT.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest and your eyes close, if that's comfortable. Let one name come up: someone you haven't forgiven. It doesn't need to be the biggest one. When the face appears, notice what happens in the body: the jaw, the chest, the hands. You don't have to forgive them now. You don't have to do anything at all. Just say the name to yourself, quietly, and let it sit beside you for a while, like someone on the next seat of a bus. If you pray, you can bring that name into your prayer, just as it is. The bell holds the time.
Forgiveness. Giving up the claim to get even, freely given, never forced, and often slow. Today's word.
Your line: sending a guard away from his post. Today, keep the name you chose nearby, and don't push. Just notice when it comes up, and what it asks of you. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

940.title: Teshuvah, the return
940.hook: Jewish repentance is a turning back, always possible
940.howItsDone: Jews speak of teshuvah all year, and especially in the month of Elul and the Days of Awe before Yom Kippur, when the liturgy returns again and again to turning back to God and repairing wrongs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forgiveness, and one name held quietly beside you. Your line was sending a guard away from his post. Did that name come back during the day? Today, the first of the Jewish voices, and a word about turning around. Day nine hundred forty.

A driver misses the exit. The map on the phone doesn't scold. It doesn't replay the mistake or call the driver careless. It just says: make a U-turn when possible. There's a quiet mercy in those last two words. When possible. The way back is still there, a little further down the road. Jewish tradition has a word for that kind of turn, and it's where these Jewish voices on forgiveness begin. Before anyone asks how to forgive someone else, this word asks something simpler: what happens when you're the one who went the wrong way?
screen: `A MISSED EXIT.` → `U-TURN WHEN POSSIBLE.` → `THE WAY BACK IS STILL THERE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Teshuvah is usually translated repentance, but its plain meaning is return: a turning back, the way you'd turn toward home after walking the wrong way. The weight falls less on feeling terrible and more on turning around. Second, the prophets' call. Hosea puts it simply, in the King James words: "O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity." Fallen, yes. But the first word is return. Ezekiel goes further. In his chapter on turning, the one who turns away from wrongdoing and does what is right will live, and the old wrongs are not held against them. And Ezekiel adds a line that sounds almost like an instruction for a renovation: "make you a new heart and a new spirit." Third, a door older than the wrong. A tradition in the Talmud lists repentance among the things made before the world itself. Read one way, that's a striking claim: the way back was built before anyone had gone wrong. The return was ready first. Fourth, small turns count. Teshuvah isn't only for the great wrongs. Jewish teachers speak of it for habits too: the sharp tongue, the temper, the thing you do when you're tired. Turning once, in the moment, is already a return. It doesn't need to wait for a holy day, though, as we'll hear this week, a season of the year is set aside for it. The door, in this teaching, stays open.
screen: `TESHUVAH MEANS RETURN.` · `O ISRAEL, RETURN.` · `READY BEFORE THE WORLD.` · `SMALL TURNS COUNT.` · then, large: `RETURN.`

segments.voice: Stay where you are and let a few breaths go by. Choose one small habit you'd like to turn back from. Not your whole character: one habit. Snapping when you're tired. Scrolling past midnight. The sarcastic reply. Hold it in mind, and find where it usually begins: the moment just before. Now let that moment arrive in your mind, and this time, turn. Just a quarter turn, the way you'd turn on a path. One step back toward the person you meant to be. If you pray, you can bring this turning into your prayer, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Teshuvah. Hebrew for return: the Jewish word for repentance, a turning back that stays possible. Today's word.
Your line: return. Today, when the habit you chose shows up, turn once. Just once is a return. Day nine hundred forty.

941.title: Four steps
941.hook: Maimonides: recognize it, regret it, confess it, resolve not to repeat it (Laws of Repentance 2)
941.carry: sorrow aimed at changing the future
941.howItsDone: Jews who follow Maimonides' teaching on teshuvah include a spoken confession, called viduy, in prayer, especially on Yom Kippur, alongside regret and a resolve to change.

segments.voice: Yesterday, teshuvah: the turn back, the U-turn that stays possible. Your line was return. Did the habit show up, and did you turn once? Today, the return broken into steps. Day nine hundred forty-one.

Some apologies have the shape of an apology and almost none of the inside. Sorry you feel that way. Mistakes were made. A quick sorry tossed over the shoulder on the way out the door. The difference from the real thing is easy to hear, even when it's hard to say exactly what's missing. A rabbi, doctor and philosopher named Moses Maimonides wrote a code of Jewish law, and inside it, a section called the Laws of Repentance. In it he takes the return we met yesterday and lays it out, step by step, so you can see what's missing.
screen: `SORRY YOU FEEL THAT WAY.` → `WHAT'S MISSING?` → `MAIMONIDES LAYS IT OUT.`

segments.voice: First, recognize it. Before anything else, you stop doing the thing, and you see it for what it was. Not a misunderstanding, not bad luck. A wrong, with your name on it. Second, regret it. Maimonides wants more than a shrug. The person regrets what they did, looking back at it and feeling sorry it happened. Sorrow about the past, aimed at changing the future. Third, confess it. Here he gets concrete: the confession is spoken, said in words, out loud before God. A wrong that has been said out loud, as a sentence, is harder to blur. Fourth, resolve. You decide not to do it again, and he says the commitment should be real enough that the One who knows the heart could vouch for it. Then he gives a test for when the return is complete. The same situation comes back. The same chance, the same strength, the same temptation. And this time, the person doesn't do it, because they've changed, not because they couldn't. And one sharp image. Confessing without resolving to stop, Maimonides says, is like someone who goes into a purifying bath while still holding the very thing that made them impure. The water can't help while your hand is still closed around it. These four steps, in his telling, are between a person and God. When the wrong was done to another person, there's something more, and that's tomorrow.
screen: `RECOGNIZE IT.` · `REGRET IT.` · `CONFESS IT ALOUD.` · `RESOLVE NOT TO REPEAT IT.` · then, large: `THE SAME CHANCE, AND YOU DON'T.`

segments.voice: Settle in for a moment, and choose one thing. Not the worst thing you've ever done. Something small and real from this week. Now walk it through the four steps, slowly. Recognize it: name it plainly to yourself, without excuses. Regret it: let yourself feel the weight of it for a breath or two, no more. Confess it: say it, even in a whisper, in a single sentence. If you pray, you can say that sentence to God. Resolve: decide what you'll do the next time the same moment comes. Then breathe out, and let your hands open in your lap. The bell holds the time.
Four steps. Maimonides' shape for teshuvah: recognize it, regret it, confess it, resolve not to repeat it. Today's word.
Your line: sorrow aimed at changing the future. Today, if the moment you chose comes back, notice it, and see whether the fourth step holds. Day nine hundred forty-one.

decide not to do it again

942.title: Ask them first
942.hook: the Day of Atonement atones for wrongs against God; wrongs against people need their forgiveness (Mishnah Yoma 8:9)
942.howItsDone: Before Yom Kippur, some Jews seek out family, friends and colleagues to ask forgiveness directly, following the Mishnah's teaching that the day does not atone for wrongs against people until the person is reconciled.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four steps from Maimonides: recognize, regret, confess, resolve. Your line was sorrow aimed at changing the future. Did the moment you chose come back? Today, the step that can't be taken alone. Day nine hundred forty-two.

It's Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, and a man has been in synagogue since the evening before. He's fasting. He's standing for the long prayers. He's said the confession, beating his chest at every line. And somewhere across town is his sister, whom he hasn't spoken to since a bad argument last spring. He's been thinking about her all day. The Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish law, has a sentence for exactly this man. It says the day he's keeping can do a great deal. But there's one thing it won't do for him.
screen: `FASTING, PRAYING, CONFESSING.` → `A SISTER ACROSS TOWN.` → `ONE THING THE DAY WON'T DO.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In the tractate on Yom Kippur, the Mishnah says it plainly: for wrongs between a person and God, the Day of Atonement atones. For wrongs between a person and another person, the Day of Atonement does not atone, until the one who did wrong makes peace with the one they wronged. Second, where it comes from. The Mishnah names Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, reading a verse from Leviticus about the day. In the King James, the verse ends: "that ye may be clean from all your sins before the LORD." He reads those last words closely. Before the Lord. The day cleanses what lies between you and God. What lies between you and your sister stays where it is until you go to her. Third, how far you have to go. Maimonides, in his Laws of Repentance, makes it practical. You go to the person and ask. If they refuse, you go back with others, a second time and a third. If they still refuse, he says, you may stop, and now the one refusing carries the fault. The asking is required. The answer is theirs. Fourth, why it matters. This teaching makes a claim about God and about people at once. In the Mishnah's reading, God doesn't do your apologizing for you. The person you hurt isn't skipped over on the way to heaven. And so, on the day before Yom Kippur, some Jews make a point of calling, writing, or knocking on a door.
screen: `THE DAY ATONES FOR SOME WRONGS.` · `BEFORE THE LORD.` · `GO, AND GO AGAIN.` · `GOD WON'T APOLOGIZE FOR YOU.` · then, large: `ASK THEM FIRST.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap. Bring to mind one person you owe an apology to. Someone who could actually hear it from you: by phone, in a message, in person. Now find the plain words. Not the long explanation. Not the reasons. Just what you did, and that you're sorry, in a sentence or two. Say them to yourself until they sound true. Then decide when, and how, you'll say them to the person. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for the courage to go. The bell holds the time.
Yom Kippur. The Mishnah's teaching: the Day of Atonement atones for wrongs against God, but wrongs against people need the person you wronged. Today's word.
Your line: the answer is theirs. Today, say the plain words to the person you chose, directly, not through someone else. Day nine hundred forty-two.

943.title: Joseph weeps
943.hook: Joseph reveals himself to the brothers who sold him, and weeps (Genesis 45:1–15)
943.howItsDone: Jews read the story of Joseph and his brothers in the weekly Torah portions in synagogue, and Christians read it in Genesis too; it is often taught as a story of reconciliation within a family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah's rule for wrongs against people: the answer is theirs. Did you say the plain words? Today, the other side of the table: a man who was wronged, and his brothers standing in front of him. Day nine hundred forty-three.

Egypt. A room in the governor's house. The brothers from Canaan stand before the governor of Egypt, and they're terrified. A silver cup was found in the sack of the youngest, Benjamin, and now the governor means to keep him as a slave. Judah steps forward and offers himself instead. He can't go home without the boy, he says; it would kill their old father. What the brothers don't know is that the governor understands every word. He is Joseph, the brother they sold into slavery years ago. And he has just reached the end of what he can hold in.
screen: `A ROOM IN EGYPT.` → `JUDAH OFFERS HIMSELF.` → `THE GOVERNOR IS JOSEPH.`

segments.voice: First, the room empties. In the King James words: "Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him; and he cried, Cause every man to go out from me." He sends the Egyptians out. Whatever happens next, he won't make his brothers face it in front of strangers. Second, the sound. "And he wept aloud: and the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard." This isn't the first time. Earlier in the story he turned away from them to weep, and once he hurried out to find a private room. This time there's nowhere to hide it, and he doesn't try. Then the words, as plain as they could be: "I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt." He names exactly what they did. Third, what he does with it. The brothers can't answer. So Joseph keeps talking: don't be grieved, he tells them, nor angry with yourselves, and he says God sent him ahead to keep people alive through the famine. Readers disagree about this. Some hear deep forgiveness. Some notice he never says the words I forgive you, and that later in Genesis, after their father dies, the brothers are afraid all over again. The text lets both readings stand. Fourth, the last line. Joseph kisses each of them and weeps on them. Then the text says: "and after that his brethren talked with him." After the tears, talking. It's a small phrase, and it may be the whole point. Years of silence, and then a family in one room, speaking again.
screen: `CAUSE EVERY MAN TO GO OUT.` · `HE WEPT ALOUD.` · `I AM JOSEPH YOUR BROTHER.` · `AFTER THAT, THEY TALKED.` · then, large: `HE WEPT ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind someone who hurt you, and choose someone where the hurt is real but not the deepest one. Let their face come. Notice whatever rises when it does, in the hands or the stomach or the breath. You don't have to push it away. Just let it soften by one degree. Breathe out, and let the shoulders drop a little. You're not saying it was fine. Like Joseph, you can name exactly what happened and still let something loosen. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, just as they are. The bell holds the time.
Joseph weeps. Face to face with the brothers who sold him, Joseph sends the room out, weeps aloud, and names who he is. Today's word.
Your line: he wept aloud. Today, when you think of the person you chose, let your shoulders drop one degree, and notice what changes. Day nine hundred forty-three.

944.title: Esau runs
944.hook: twenty years after being cheated, Esau runs to embrace Jacob (Genesis 33:4)
944.howItsDone: Jews read the meeting of Jacob and Esau in the yearly cycle of Torah readings in synagogue, and Christians read it in Genesis; it is taught as a story of brothers reconciled after a deep wrong.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph in a room in Egypt. Your line was he wept aloud. Did your shoulders drop, even one degree? Today, another pair of brothers in Genesis, and this time, the wronged one runs. Day nine hundred forty-four.

Dust on the horizon. Jacob looks up, and there is his brother Esau, and with him, the text says, four hundred men. The last time they were together, Jacob dressed up as Esau, fooled their blind father, and walked off with the blessing meant for his brother. Esau said in his heart that he would kill him. Jacob ran, and stayed away a long time; in his own words to his father-in-law, twenty years. Now he's coming home, and he's limping from a night of wrestling by the river. He has sent gifts ahead, flocks and herds, wave after wave. He has split his camp in two, in case one half is attacked. And now he walks out in front of them all.
screen: `DUST ON THE HORIZON.` → `THE STOLEN BLESSING.` → `JACOB WALKS OUT IN FRONT.`

segments.voice: First, Jacob bows. The King James says he "bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother." It's the posture of a man expecting the worst and hoping to soften it. Second, Esau runs. And here is the whole surprise, in one verse: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." No speech first. No terms. No demand for an apology. The text never says what changed in Esau over those years. It only shows us his feet. Third, the gifts. Jacob keeps pressing the flocks on him, and Esau waves them off: "I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself." Jacob won't let it go. "Take, I pray thee, my blessing that is brought to thee." Some readers notice the word. Blessing. The very thing he stole years before, and here he is, trying to hand a blessing back. Fourth, a face. Jacob says something strange to his brother: "I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God." The night before, he had wrestled until dawn and named the place for seeing God face to face. Now he says the same thing about his brother's face. Readers have heard different things in that line. One reading: a face that should have been angry and is kind instead is about as close to the divine as it gets. The story doesn't tie a bow on it. The brothers part ways again soon after. But for one morning, the wronged one ran.
screen: `SEVEN TIMES TO THE GROUND.` · `ESAU RAN TO MEET HIM.` · `I HAVE ENOUGH, MY BROTHER.` · `AS THOUGH THE FACE OF GOD.` · then, large: `HE RAN TO MEET HIM.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone you've drifted from: a brother or sister, a cousin, an old friend, someone where things went quiet after a hurt, on either side. You don't have to fix the whole story. Ask only this: what is one step toward them? A message that just says hello. A photo you could send. A question about their kids. Choose the smallest step that's still a step. Hold it, and let your feet feel the floor, as if they're ready to move. If you pray, you can hold this person in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Esau runs. Years after Jacob cheated him of the blessing, Esau runs to meet his brother, embraces him, and they weep. Today's word.
Your line: he ran to meet him. Today, take the one small step you chose toward that person. Not the whole way. One step. Day nine hundred forty-four.

945.title: The Days of Awe
945.hook: ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur for making amends
945.howItsDone: During the Days of Awe, Jews pray special prayers, hear the shofar on Rosh Hashanah, give charity, and seek out people they have wronged to ask forgiveness before Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Esau runs: the wronged brother moving first. Your line was he ran to meet him. Did you take your one small step? Today, the end of the week, and a season built for everything we've heard in it. Day nine hundred forty-five.

Two dates circled on a kitchen calendar. Next to the first, someone has drawn a little ram's horn. Next to the second, a single word: fast. Between them, the squares are full of small notes. Call Mom. Coffee with Dan. Write to Mr. Levin. Return the drill. It looks like an ordinary to-do list. It isn't. It's a list of people. In the Jewish year, the stretch between those two circles has a name, and it's built for exactly what this week has been about: turning back, and going to the people you've wronged.
screen: `TWO DATES CIRCLED.` → `A LIST OF PEOPLE.` → `A SEASON FOR TURNING BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the calendar. Leviticus sets the two days. In the King James words: "In the seventh month, in the first day of the month, shall ye have a sabbath, a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation." That's the day Jews call Rosh Hashanah, the new year. And then: "Also on the tenth day of this seventh month there shall be a day of atonement." Yom Kippur. From the first day to the tenth: ten days. In Hebrew they're called the Yamim Noraim, the Days of Awe. Second, the picture. Tradition says, in a teaching in the Talmud, that on the new year the books are opened, and on the Day of Atonement they're sealed. Those in between have until then. It's an image, and readers hold it in different ways, but it gives the days their feel: a door that's open, and won't stay open forever. Third, the work. A prayer in the liturgy for these days names three things that turn aside the harsh decree: repentance, prayer and charity. Teshuvah, which opened this week. Prayer. And giving. Fourth, this whole week in one season. Forgiveness. The turn back. Maimonides' four steps. Asking the person first. Joseph weeping. Esau running. Joseph and Esau are read at other times of the year, but the turning, the steps and the asking all come due in these ten days. That's what the season is for: the apology that's been waiting, the call you keep putting off, made inside a window with a closing date, before the second circle on the calendar.
